subject: mathematics
question_text: If A + B + C = π, then prove that cos²(A/2) + cos²(B/2) + cos²(C/2) = 2(1 + sin(A/2) sin(B/2) sin(C/2)).

mark_split.label: Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula
Apply the product formula and conclude

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.41 — LAQ chapter 5 T-Ratios upto Transformations, answer 28, on a ★★★ SSP (Super Scoring Page). Printed appearances: AP 15,16 · TS 15,17. The answer has a 2 outside the whole bracket, which is unusual — it appears because the constant that survives is 2, not 1. The book notes it rains marks in the IPE. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed anywhere in this chapter (its pages are set two questions to a page in two columns, which takes the margin those tags would occupy). The SAME split and the SAME step ids are used on all eight answers in this chapter, deliberately: they are ONE method over different identities — pair two terms, use the angle condition, factor, finish with a product formula. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say the four moves in order, and where the angle condition gets used.

steps.label: State the angle condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. π is 180°, so this is the same halved condition as the previous two questions written in radians.
steps.memory_tip: π is 180°, so this is the halved condition written in radians: (A+B)/2 = π/2 − C/2.

recall.must_convey: That the angle condition is written down first, in the form the proof will actually use.
accept: write the angle condition first in the form the proof needs
state the given condition and rearrange it
note the angle sum before starting the transformation
modata angle condition rasi, kavalsina form lo pettali
write down the condition on the angles

steps.why: Without the condition the statement is simply false, so it is not preamble — it is the hypothesis the whole proof leans on, and it is used at least twice below.
common_mistakes: Starting the transformation before writing the condition.
Writing the condition but never rearranging it into a usable form.

steps.label: Pair two terms
steps.margin_note: Three of the eight marks. Three terms will not factorise as they stand, so two of them are combined into a product first. Quote the formula in brackets — the formulas are what the examiner marks.
steps.memory_tip: Three terms will not factorise as they stand, so combine TWO into a product first. Quote the formula.

recall.must_convey: That one squared cosine is written as 1 − sin² so a difference of squares appears, producing a leading 1.
accept: write cos squared B over two as one minus sin squared so a difference of squares appears
convert one term to make a one and a difference of squares
replace the middle term with one minus sine squared
rendo term ni one minus sin square ga rasta
turn one cosine squared into one minus sine squared

steps.why: Two constants appear in this proof — this 1 and another later — and together they make the 2 that sits outside the answer.

steps.label: Use the condition
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. This is where the angle condition earns its place: it converts an expression in A and B into one in C, so that every term shares a factor.
steps.memory_tip: The condition turns an expression in A and B into one in C, so every term shares a factor.

recall.must_convey: That the identity is applied, cos((A+B)/2) becomes sin(C/2), and cos²(C/2) is written as 1 − sin²(C/2) — producing the second constant that makes the 2.
accept: apply the identity, convert to sin C over two, and write cos squared C over two as one minus sin squared so the constant becomes two
the two ones add to give the two outside the answer
convert the last cosine squared as well and the constants add
rendu ones kalisi two avthundi
the second one comes from cos squared C over two

steps.why: This is where the 2 in the answer comes from: one constant from the first conversion and one from the second, added together.
common_mistakes: Leaving cos²(C/2) alone and never producing the second 1.

steps.label: Take the common factor out
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. The common factor comes out, and the condition is used a SECOND time inside the bracket so that both bracket terms are the same kind of function.
steps.memory_tip: Pull the common factor out, then use the condition a SECOND time inside the bracket.

recall.must_convey: That sin(C/2) is taken out, leaving a difference of two cosines in the bracket.
accept: take sin C over two common leaving a difference of cosines in the bracket
factor out sin C over two and convert the second term back to a cosine
the bracket becomes cos A minus B over two minus cos A plus B over two
sin C by two common teesi bracket lo cosines ga marchali
both bracket terms become cosines

steps.why: The 2 plays no further part, so setting it aside keeps the factorisation clean — the same tactic as the −1 in answer 26.2.
common_mistakes: Trying to factor the 2 into the bracket.
Leaving a sine inside the bracket so no formula applies.

steps.label: Apply the product formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. One more sum-or-difference formula turns the bracket into a product, and the identity closes. Write "= R.H.S" so the examiner can see it landed.
steps.memory_tip: One more sum-or-difference formula closes it. Write '= R.H.S' so the examiner sees it landed.

recall.must_convey: That the bracket becomes 2 sin(A/2) sin(B/2), and that a final 2 is taken out to match the required form.
accept: the bracket gives two sin A over two sin B over two and then take two out to match the answer
finish with the cosine difference formula then factor the two out
take two common at the end to get two into one plus the product
chivarlo two common teeste required form vasthundi
factor out the two to match the right hand side

steps.why: The answer was asked for in the factored form 2(1 + …), so the last line has to produce that form rather than 2 + 2(…).
